# Education in Poland: Summary
Education in Poland is structured into compulsory and post-compulsory stages. Children typically enter primary school at age seven (or six in certain cases), completing eight years of primary education. Prior to reforms in 2017, this consisted of six years of primary school followed by three years of gimnazjum (junior high school), but gimnazjum was abolished and replaced by the current eight-year primary system. After primary education, students pursue upper secondary education via general secondary schools (liceum), technical schools (technikum), or basic vocational schools, which prepare them either for direct entry into the workforce or further academic study. The Matura exam at the end of general and technical secondary education allows access to higher education.
Tertiary education follows the Bologna framework, generally consisting of a three-year bachelor's degree and a two-year master's degree, with some integrated longer master's programs for fields like medicine or pharmacy. Doctoral programs typically require about three years of study. Foreign languages are emphasized— the majority of students study English, German, or other languages. Historical commitment to education in Poland is notable, with the Jagiellonian University founded in 1364 and compulsory education officially established in the early 20th century. Modern reforms have aimed to improve educational outcomes, increase time spent on core subjects, and enhance performance in international assessments. The grading system at universities ranges numerically from 2 (fail) to 5 (excellent), with nuanced increments. Education for national minorities and students with disabilities is provided, and violence prevention and teacher protections have been reinforced in recent years.
